posts.title: The Surfer's Guide to Recovery in Lagos, Portugal: Why Yoga Is the Missing Piece
posts.description: You paddle all morning. Your shoulders ache. Your lower back is tight. Your hips feel like they're locked in place. Here's exactly why surfing destroys your body and how the right recovery work at Heat Lagos keeps you in the water every day.
posts.lede: I moved to Lagos because of the surf. Within two weeks, I couldn't paddle without shoulder pain. Within a month, my lower back was so tight I could barely bend over to put on my wetsuit. I thought this was normal — surfers hurt. That's just part of the deal. But it's not normal. And it's not part of the deal. Here's what I learned about keeping your body in the water for decades, not just seasons.

content.text: What Surfing Does to Your Body

Surfing is a one-sided, repetitive sport that tightens the front of your body and weakens the back. Paddling loads the shoulders and chest. Looking forward for waves shortens the neck flexors. The pop-up demands explosive hip extension from a position of spinal extension. And duck-diving under waves compresses the entire spine.

Over time, this creates a predictable pattern: rounded shoulders, forward head posture, tight hip flexors, and a lower back that's constantly in extension. This pattern leads to shoulder impingement, lower back pain, hip tightness, and eventually — time off the water.
The Daily Surfer's Recovery Routine
10 minutes. Every day. No excuses. Whether you surfed or not.

items: Child's pose with side bends (2 min): Opens the lats and decompresses the spine after paddling.
Chest opener over a foam roller (2 min): Reverse the hunched paddling posture. Lie lengthwise over a foam roller, arms open like a T. Breathe deeply.
Figure 4 glute stretch (2 min per side): Releases the piriformis, which tightens from the paddling hip position.
Spinal twist (90 sec per side): Unwinds the rotational loading from pop-ups and cutbacks.
Deep breathing in corpse pose (2 min): Activates the parasympathetic nervous system for recovery.

content.text: Heating up vs. cooling down: There's a common myth that surfing is a "cool-down" activity for surfers who just trained. Actually, surfing IS the training. What you need after is not more movement — it's targeted release and recovery work. That's where infrared heat comes in. The far infrared wavelengths penetrate deep into muscle tissue, increasing blood flow and reducing inflammation without adding mechanical load.
Why Infrared Recovery Works for Surfers

Traditional recovery for surfers means foam rolling and static stretching. These work, but they're limited by how much time you can spend on them. Infrared heating adds a deeper layer: the heat penetrates 1.5 inches into muscle tissue, promoting vasodilation and flushing metabolic waste products like lactic acid.

This is especially valuable for surfers because surf recovery is about low-grade systemic inflammation — the kind that accumulates over a surf trip or a season. Infrared heat addresses this at the cellular level.
The Infrared Recovery Class at Heat Lagos

Our Heat Recovery class combines mobility, breathwork, long yin holds, and guided deep rest in our infrared-heated studio. It's designed specifically for people who load their bodies during the day — surfers, runners, yoga practitioners, and anyone living an active lifestyle in the Algarve.

45 minutes. No intense movement. Just deep, therapeutic release. The heat supports muscle relaxation. The breathwork shifts your nervous system into rest-and-digest mode. The stillness allows your body to actually repair.

posts.title: Why Choose Infrared Hot Pilates Over Traditional Pilates? (The Science of the Difference)
posts.description: Infrared Pilates vs. traditional Pilates — what's the actual difference? Here's the science behind far-infrared heating, why it's gentler than hot yoga, and why our members at Heat Lagos see faster results.
posts.lede: When I opened Heat Lagos, the most common question was: "What's the difference between your Pilates class and a normal Pilates class?" The honest answer is: the heat changes everything. Not in the way you might think — it's not just about sweating more. The infrared heat changes how your muscles work, how your joints move, and how your body recovers.

content.text: What Infrared Heating Actually Does

Unlike traditional hot yoga which uses forced air heating (blowing hot air around the room), our infrared panels heat objects and bodies directly. The room air is around 30°C — warm but not oppressive. The difference is that the heat is working at a deeper level.

Far-infrared wavelengths penetrate up to 1.5 inches into tissue. This means your muscles are being heated from the inside out, not from the skin in. The result: better blood flow, increased tissue elasticity, and reduced muscle tension before you even start moving.
Traditional Hot Yoga vs Infrared Difference

Traditional hot yoga rooms are heated to 38-42°C with high humidity. This can be overwhelming — especially for beginners. The heat comes from the air, which means you're breathing hot air, which puts stress on your cardiovascular system before you even start practicing.

Infrared heating at 30°C is dramatically different. The air is comfortable. You can breathe easily. But your body is still getting the deep heating effect on your muscles. This makes infrared suitable for a much wider range of people — from elite athletes to people recovering from injury.
Three Benefits of Infrared Pilates
1. Deeper Muscle Activation

Heat increases muscle pliability, which allows for a fuller range of motion during exercises. In Pilates, range of motion is critical for proper muscle engagement. The infrared heat means you're getting more out of every movement.
2. Improved Recovery

The enhanced blood flow from infrared heat means metabolic waste products (like the lactic acid that causes soreness) are cleared more efficiently. Our members consistently report less DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) after infrared classes compared to non-heated classes.
3. Greater Mind-Body Connection

The warmth is grounding. It creates a sensory-rich environment that helps you stay present in your body. This is especially valuable in Pilates, where proprioception and body awareness are the foundation of good form.
